questions.stem_md: What is the basic event in reproduction?

options.text_md: Growth of the body to its full size
Making a copy of the DNA
Making food by photosynthesis
Division of the cytoplasm without the nucleus

questions.solution_md: Reproduction begins with the cell making a copy of its DNA (with extra cell apparatus) and then dividing, so each new cell gets a copy — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Why are offspring produced from a single parent similar to it, but not exactly identical?

options.text_md: They receive DNA from two different parents.
The environment rewrites their DNA every day.
Cells divide without copying their DNA.
DNA copying is not perfectly accurate, so small changes creep in.

questions.solution_md: With a single parent there is no mixing of DNA; the small differences come from slight inaccuracies each time DNA is copied — option (d). (a) describes sexual reproduction; (b) and (c) are not true.

questions.stem_md: During a heat wave, the water of a village pond becomes several degrees warmer. Most of the bacteria in it die, but a few survive and soon multiply. What is the best explanation?

options.text_md: A few bacteria already had variations that let them tolerate heat, and they passed these on.
The heat made all the bacteria produce heat-resistant DNA on purpose.
Only the largest bacteria survived, because size protects against heat.
The survivors stopped reproducing so that they could save energy.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Copying errors over many generations had already produced slightly different bacteria.

Step 2 — Those that happened to tolerate heat survived and reproduced, passing on the variation — option (a).

Step 3 — Variations are not made to order by the environment (b); size (c) and stopping reproduction (d) do not explain survival and multiplication.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Variation helps a species survive when its surroundings change drastically.

**Reason (R):** Some individuals in a varied population may have features that suit the new conditions.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Because some varied individuals may suit the new conditions, they survive and keep the species going, so R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? DNA copying during reproduction always produces exact copies.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. DNA copying is very accurate but not perfect; the small changes produce variation.

questions.stem_md: Explain why (a) consistency in DNA copying is important for a species, and (b) a small amount of variation is also useful.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Consistent copying keeps the **body design** that suits the organism to its **niche**, so offspring can live where their parents live.

(b) If the niche changes drastically, a few individuals with **suitable variations** may survive, so the species is not wiped out.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Consistency maintains a working body design for the niche.

Step 2 — Variation allows survival when the niche changes.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Consistency keeps the body design suited to the niche
(b) Variation lets some survive a changed niche

questions.stem_md:
A farmer has two fields of the same fodder grass. Field A was planted only from runners (stem pieces) of a single plant; field B was grown from seeds collected from many plants. A new fungal disease reaches the area.

(a) In which field is the grass more likely to survive the disease? 

(b) Explain your answer in terms of variation.

(c) Give one advantage that field A still has.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Field B**.

(b) Plants grown from runners of one plant are genetically almost identical, so if the disease can attack one, it can attack all. Seeds come from sexual reproduction among many plants, so field B has much more **variation**; some plants are likely to resist the disease and survive.

(c) Field A’s plants keep all the good qualities of the parent plant and grow quickly (vegetative propagation).

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Identify the method of reproduction in each field.

Step 2 — Link variation to the chance that some plants resist the disease.

Step 3 — Recall an advantage of vegetative propagation.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Field B has more variation; some plants may resist
(c) One valid advantage of field A

questions.stem_md: Amoeba reproduces asexually by:

options.text_md: budding
multiple fission
binary fission
spore formation

questions.solution_md: Amoeba splits into two equal daughter cells: binary fission — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The malaria parasite Plasmodium reproduces by:

options.text_md: binary fission
fragmentation
multiple fission
budding

questions.solution_md: Plasmodium divides into many daughter cells at once: multiple fission — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A sample from a kala-azar patient shows Leishmania cells, each with a whip-like structure at one end, about to divide. How will each cell divide?

options.text_md: Into two cells, along any plane at random
Into many cells at once inside a cyst
Into two cells, along a definite plane related to the whip-like structure
By forming a small bud that later detaches

questions.solution_md: Leishmania reproduces by binary fission, and because of the whip-like structure the split happens in a definite orientation — option (c). Splitting in any plane (a) describes Amoeba; a cyst with many cells (b) is multiple fission in Plasmodium; budding (d) is seen in Hydra and yeast.

questions.stem_md: A student notices that a mature filament of Spirogyra in a pond has broken into several pieces, and each piece is growing into a new filament. This is:

options.text_md: regeneration
budding
fragmentation
spore formation

questions.solution_md: A simple multicellular organism that breaks into pieces on maturing, each growing into a new individual, shows fragmentation — option (c). Regeneration (a) is the rebuilding of a whole body from a cut piece by specialised cells.

questions.stem_md: In July, a slice of bread left in a damp kitchen develops fuzzy black patches within three days, but a slice of the same bread kept dry in a sealed box stays clean. What best explains this?

options.text_md: Bread itself turns into mould when it becomes warm.
Spores of bread mould from the air germinate only on moist surfaces.
Mould needs light, and the box was dark.
Dry bread contains no food that mould can use.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Mould spores are present in the air; they germinate when they land on a moist surface with food.

Step 2 — The damp slice was moist, the dry slice was not — option (b).

Step 3 — Bread does not turn into mould (a); light is not the deciding factor (c); dry bread still contains food (d).

questions.stem_md: Why do farmers grow bananas from suckers (side shoots) rather than from seeds?

options.text_md: Cultivated bananas do not produce viable seeds.
Banana seeds are poisonous to the soil.
Plants grown from seeds give more fruit each year.
Suckers produce plants with more variation.

questions.solution_md: Cultivated bananas have lost the capacity to produce seeds, so they are propagated vegetatively — option (a). Vegetative propagation gives less variation, not more (d).

questions.stem_md: A new rust disease is damaging wheat in Punjab. Plant breeders want new wheat plants, some of which may resist the disease. Which way of producing plants gives them the best chance?

options.text_md: Cross-pollinating different varieties and growing the seeds, since this mixes DNA from two parents
Growing many stem cuttings from one healthy plant
Grafting shoots of one plant onto many rootstocks
Allowing one plant to self-propagate by fragments

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Resistance can only be found if the new plants vary.

Step 2 — Sexual reproduction combines DNA from two parents and produces new combinations, giving the most variation — option (a).

Step 3 — Cuttings, grafts and fragments (b, c, d) are vegetative copies of one plant, so they carry no new variation.

questions.stem_md: Planaria can regrow a whole body from a small piece. Why is regeneration still not counted as the normal way of reproducing for most organisms?

options.text_md: Regenerated worms are not alive.
Regenerated worms can never reproduce again.
Regeneration happens only in plants.
Most organisms do not depend on being cut into pieces in order to reproduce.

questions.solution_md: Regeneration rebuilds a body from a piece, but organisms do not normally rely on being cut up to make offspring — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A nursery owner in Ratnagiri wants hundreds of Alphonso mango saplings that will all give fruit of exactly the same taste as his best tree, and bear fruit years sooner than seedlings. Which method should he use?

options.text_md: Grafting shoots of the best tree onto young rooted plants
Sowing seeds from the best tree’s fruits
Cross-pollinating the best tree with other varieties
Planting leaves of the best tree in moist soil

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Identical quality and early fruiting point to vegetative propagation.

Step 2 — Mango is propagated by grafting — option (a).

Step 3 — Seeds (b) and cross-pollination (c) involve sexual reproduction and give variation; mango leaves (d) do not grow into new plants.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Plasmodium reproduces by binary fission.

**Reason (R):** In multiple fission, one cell divides into many daughter cells at the same time.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: Plasmodium reproduces by multiple fission. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Hydra can reproduce by budding.

**Reason (R):** In budding, the parent splits into two equal halves.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: in budding a small outgrowth forms and detaches; splitting into two equal halves is binary fission — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In bread mould, spores are formed inside round structures on stalks called ___.
questions.solution_md: The spores are formed in **sporangia**.

questions.stem_md: A bacterium divides by binary fission every 20 minutes, and each daughter does the same. Starting with one bacterium, how many bacteria will there be after 2 hours (if none die)?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Number of divisions $= \dfrac{120}{20} = 6$.

Step 2 — Each division doubles the number, so after 6 divisions there are $2^6 = 64$ bacteria.

marking_scheme.step: Finds 6 divisions and 2 to the power 6 = 64

questions.stem_md: Match each organism in Column A with its method of asexual reproduction in Column B.

options.text_md: Amoeba
Plasmodium
Spirogyra
Rhizopus

questions.solution_md: Amoeba → binary fission (1 → r); Plasmodium → multiple fission (2 → p); Spirogyra → fragmentation (3 → s); Rhizopus → spore formation (4 → q).

questions.stem_md: Describe budding in Hydra. How is it different from binary fission in Amoeba?

answer.model_answer_md: In Hydra, cells divide repeatedly at one spot to form a small outgrowth, the **bud**. It grows tentacles and, when mature, **detaches** as a new Hydra. In **binary fission**, the whole parent cell splits into **two equal** daughter cells, so the parent no longer exists as such; in budding the parent remains and the bud is smaller at first.

questions.solution_md: Describe the bud forming and detaching, then contrast it with equal splitting.

questions.stem_md: A farmer in Agra cuts a large potato into pieces, each with an "eye", and plants them. (a) Why does each piece grow into a new plant? (b) Why will all the new plants give potatoes of the same quality as the parent?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A potato is a swollen underground **stem**, and each eye is a **bud** that can sprout into a shoot and roots: this is vegetative propagation.

(b) The new plants come from the parent’s own body without germ cells, so they are **genetically similar** to the parent and keep its qualities.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — The eye is a bud on a stem tuber.

Step 2 — Vegetative propagation gives offspring genetically similar to the parent.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Eye is a bud on a stem, so it sprouts

questions.stem_md: A microbiologist looks at three slides. Slide 1: a cell splitting into two, in any direction. Slide 2: a cell with a whip-like structure at one end, splitting into two along a fixed line. Slide 3: a thick-walled cyst bursting to release many small cells. For each slide, name the method of reproduction and a likely organism.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Slide 1:** binary fission (division in any plane) — **Amoeba**.

**Slide 2:** binary fission in a definite plane — **Leishmania**.

**Slide 3:** multiple fission inside a cyst — **Plasmodium** (malaria parasite).

questions.solution_md: Use the number of daughter cells and the plane of division to identify each method and organism.

marking_scheme.step: Slide 2: binary fission in a definite plane, Leishmania

questions.stem_md:
Ritika wants more plants of her grandmother’s fragrant rose bush, which rarely sets seed. A gardener suggests planting stem cuttings.

(a) What kind of reproduction is this?

(b) Give two reasons why it suits Ritika’s aim.

(c) Suggest one disadvantage if all her rose plants come from this one bush.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Vegetative propagation** — asexual reproduction from a stem.

(b) The new plants will have the **same fragrance and qualities** as the grandmother’s bush, and they will **flower sooner** than plants grown from seed; it also works even though the bush rarely sets seed.

(c) All the plants will be almost identical, so a **disease or pest** that attacks one is likely to attack all of them.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Name the method.

Step 2 — Match its advantages to her aim.

Step 3 — Lack of variation is the main disadvantage.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Lack of variation, so disease can affect all

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is asexual reproduction?

(b) With labelled diagrams, describe (i) binary fission in Amoeba and (ii) spore formation in Rhizopus.

(c) Why are plants such as banana and jasmine grown by vegetative propagation?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Asexual reproduction is the production of new individuals from a **single parent**, without germ cells; the offspring are nearly identical to the parent.

(b) (i) Diagram stages: parent cell with nucleus → nucleus divides → cytoplasm divides → two daughter cells. The Amoeba copies its DNA, the nucleus divides and then the cytoplasm splits into two equal halves. (ii) Diagram labels: hyphae, sporangium, spores. Rhizopus forms sporangia on upright stalks; they contain many spores with thick walls. When released, spores that reach a moist surface with food germinate into new moulds.

(c) These plants have **lost the capacity to produce seeds**, so vegetative propagation is the only practical way to grow them; it also keeps the parent’s qualities and gives earlier flowering.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Define asexual reproduction.

Step 2 — Draw and describe the two processes stage by stage.

Step 3 — Link seedlessness to vegetative propagation.

marking_scheme.step: (c) No viable seeds (plus one other advantage)

questions.stem_md: Which part of a flower produces pollen grains?

options.text_md: Stigma
Ovary
Anther
Filament

questions.solution_md: The anther, at the top of the stamen, produces pollen grains — option (c). The filament (d) only holds up the anther.

questions.stem_md: Ajay plants a single watermelon vine. The first flowers that open all have stamens but no pistil. What can he conclude?

options.text_md: They will each develop into a watermelon after pollination.
They are male flowers; only flowers with a pistil can develop into fruits.
They are bisexual flowers that have lost their pistils.
The vine can never form fruit, because its flowers are male.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Watermelon has unisexual flowers: male flowers have only stamens, female flowers have a pistil.

Step 2 — A fruit develops from an ovary, which is part of the pistil, so these male flowers cannot become fruits — option (b).

Step 3 — The same vine also produces female flowers later, so (d) is wrong; they are not damaged bisexual flowers (c).

questions.stem_md: While eating a tomato, Meena notices the many small seeds inside it. Which statement about the tomato is correct?

options.text_md: The fleshy part developed from an ovule, and the seeds from the ovary.
The fleshy part developed from the petals, and the seeds from the anthers.
The fleshy part developed from the stigma, and the seeds from pollen grains.
The fleshy part developed from the ovary, and each seed from an ovule.

questions.solution_md: After fertilisation the ovary ripens into the fruit (the fleshy part) and the ovules become seeds — option (d). (a) swaps the two; petals, anthers and stigma wither (b, c).

questions.stem_md: A farmer grows only female papaya trees inside a sealed glasshouse that keeps out insects and wind. The trees flower well but bear no fruit, while female trees in an open field near male trees fruit normally. Why?

options.text_md: No pollen could reach the stigmas of the female flowers, so no fertilisation took place.
The glasshouse was too warm for the ovaries to form.
Papaya flowers pollinate themselves, so the glasshouse should not matter.
Female papaya flowers do not have ovaries.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Papaya flowers are unisexual: female flowers need pollen from male flowers.

Step 2 — With no male trees, insects or wind inside, no pollen reached the stigmas; without pollination and fertilisation the ovaries do not become fruits — option (a).

Step 3 — Unisexual flowers cannot self-pollinate (c), and female flowers do have ovaries (d).

questions.stem_md: The leaf cells of a plant have 14 chromosomes. A student claims that its male and female germ cells also have 14 chromosomes each. If this were true, what would happen?

options.text_md: The number would stay at 14 in every generation.
The number would halve every generation: 7, then 3 or 4.
Only the male germ cell’s chromosomes would reach the zygote.
The number would double every generation: 28 in the next generation, 56 in the one after, and so on.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — The zygote gets the chromosomes of both germ cells: 14 + 14 = 28, double the parent’s number.

Step 2 — Repeating this each generation doubles the number again: 56, 112 … — option (d).

Step 3 — This is why germ cells actually carry half the number (7 here), so the zygote has 14.

questions.stem_md: A bee carries pollen from a mustard flower in Harpreet’s field to a mustard flower in her neighbour’s field. This is:

options.text_md: cross-pollination
self-pollination
fertilisation
vegetative propagation

questions.solution_md: Pollen reaching the stigma of a flower on a different plant is cross-pollination — option (a). Fertilisation (c) happens later, when germ cells fuse in the ovule.

questions.stem_md: In an experiment, pollen is placed on the stigmas of several flowers, and an hour later the styles of half the flowers are cut just below the stigma. Only the uncut flowers form seeds. Why?

options.text_md: In the cut flowers the pollen tubes could not grow down to the ovules, so the male germ cells never reached the eggs.
Cutting the style removed the ovules.
Pollination needs the style, so no pollen landed on the cut flowers.
Cutting the style stopped the anthers from making pollen.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Pollination had already happened: pollen was on the stigmas.

Step 2 — The pollen tube must grow through the style to deliver the male germ cell to the ovule; cutting the style broke this path, so there was no fertilisation and no seeds — option (a).

Step 3 — The ovules are in the ovary, which was not cut (b).

questions.stem_md: Sameer grows a bean seedling on wet cotton. After ten days, the two thick cotyledons have become thin and shrivelled while the seedling has grown taller. The best explanation is that:

options.text_md: the cotyledons were attacked by bread mould
the cotyledons lost their food to the wet cotton
the food stored in the cotyledons was used by the growing seedling
cotyledons always shrivel because they are dead tissue

questions.solution_md: Cotyledons store food for the young seedling until its leaves can make food; as the stored food is used up, they shrink — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** After fertilisation, the ovary of a flower ripens into a fruit.

**Reason (R):** After fertilisation, the ovules develop into seeds.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but they are two separate changes: the ovule becoming a seed does not explain why the ovary becomes a fruit — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Germ cells contain half the number of chromosomes found in body cells.

**Reason (R):** This keeps the number of chromosomes constant from one generation to the next when two germ cells fuse.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R gives the reason for A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: After fertilisation, the ___ of the flower grows and ripens to form the fruit.
questions.solution_md: The **ovary** becomes the fruit; the ovules inside become seeds.

questions.stem_md: The body cells of a potato plant contain 48 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are present in an egg cell in one of its ovules?
questions.solution_md: A germ cell has half the chromosomes of a body cell: $\dfrac{48}{2} = 24$.

questions.stem_md: A pea pod contains 9 seeds. What is the minimum number of pollen grains that must have germinated on the stigma to produce these seeds?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Each seed develops from one fertilised ovule.

Step 2 — Each ovule needs its own male germ cell, delivered by the pollen tube of one pollen grain, so at least 9 pollen grains are needed.

marking_scheme.step: One pollen grain per fertilised ovule, so 9

questions.stem_md: Match each part of a flower in Column A with what it does or becomes in Column B.

options.text_md: Anther
Stigma
Ovule
Ovary

questions.solution_md: Anther → produces pollen (1 → s); stigma → receives pollen (2 → p); ovule → seed (3 → r); ovary → fruit (4 → q).

questions.stem_md: A farmer near Bharatpur keeps beehives beside his mustard field to get more seeds, but his neighbour’s maize crop gives a good harvest without any bees. Explain this difference in terms of pollination.

answer.model_answer_md: Mustard flowers are bright yellow, with nectar, and are **cross-pollinated by insects**: bees carry pollen between flowers, so more bees mean more pollination and more seeds. Maize is **pollinated by wind**: it releases huge amounts of light pollen that the wind carries to other plants, so it does not need bees.

questions.solution_md: Identify the pollinating agent of each crop and link it to the features of its flowers.

marking_scheme.step: Mustard: insect pollination, so bees increase seed set
Maize: wind pollination, so bees are not needed

questions.stem_md: Shruti splits open a gram seed that was soaked overnight. Name the parts she would find that will form (a) the shoot and (b) the root, and state the job of (c) the two thick halves.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The **plumule** will form the shoot.

(b) The **radicle** will form the root.

(c) The two thick halves are the **cotyledons**; they store food for the seedling until its leaves can make food.

questions.solution_md: Identify the plumule, radicle and cotyledons and their roles.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Cotyledons store food for the seedling

questions.stem_md: State what happens after fertilisation to (a) the zygote, (b) the ovule, (c) the ovary and (d) the petals and stamens.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The zygote divides many times to form the **embryo**.

(b) The ovule develops a tough coat and becomes the **seed**.

(c) The ovary grows and ripens into the **fruit**.

(d) The petals and stamens (with the sepals, style and stigma) usually **wither and fall off**.

questions.solution_md: Give the fate of each part in turn.

questions.stem_md:
A rice breeder at a research station crosses a high-yielding variety with a flood-tolerant variety, hoping to get plants that have both qualities.

(a) Why can this be done only through sexual reproduction?

(b) Why do the offspring plants differ from one another?

(c) Why must the germ cells of each parent carry half the chromosomes?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Sexual reproduction **combines DNA from two parents**, so features of both varieties can come together in one plant; asexual methods only copy one parent.

(b) Each germ cell carries a **different mix** of the parent’s DNA, and they combine in new ways at fertilisation, so the offspring show **variation**.

(c) So that when the two germ cells fuse, the zygote has the **normal number** of chromosomes, the same as each parent.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Combining DNA needs two parents.

Step 2 — New combinations give variation.

Step 3 — Halving keeps the chromosome number constant.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of the longitudinal section of a flower.

(b) What is pollination? How does the male germ cell reach the female germ cell after pollination?

(c) Describe the changes that take place in a flower after fertilisation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Diagram labels: **sepal, petal, stamen (anther and filament), pistil (stigma, style, ovary), ovule**.

(b) Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma. On the stigma, a pollen grain grows a **pollen tube** that passes down through the style to the ovule. The male germ cell travels down the tube and fuses with the female germ cell (egg) in the ovule: this is fertilisation, giving a **zygote**.

(c) The zygote divides to form an **embryo**; the ovule develops a tough coat and becomes the **seed**; the ovary grows and ripens into the **fruit**; the petals, sepals, stamens, style and stigma shrivel and fall off.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Draw and label all the parts.

Step 2 — Define pollination, then describe the pollen tube.

Step 3 — Give the fate of each part.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Pollen tube carries the male germ cell to the egg

questions.stem_md: Why are the testes located outside the abdominal cavity, in the scrotum?

options.text_md: Sperm formation needs a temperature lower than normal body temperature.
There is no space for them inside the abdomen.
They need more light to produce sperms.
They must stay close to the kidneys.

questions.solution_md: Sperms are formed best at a temperature slightly below body temperature, which the scrotum provides — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In human beings, fertilisation usually takes place in the:

options.text_md: uterus
oviduct (fallopian tube)
ovary
vagina
